title: A change in priority
stem: At the start of a shift, which client should the practical nurse assess first?
options: A client with postoperative incisional pain of 7/10, stable vital signs and prescribed analgesia due
A client with new stridor after neck surgery
A client who has not voided for six hours after catheter removal and reports bladder pressure
A client with nausea after an oral antibiotic who is alert, breathing normally and has stable vital signs
why: Pain needs prompt treatment, but new stridor represents a more immediate airway threat.
New stridor suggests upper-airway obstruction. Assess immediately and activate appropriate emergency help.
Possible retention needs assessment, after the immediate airway threat is addressed.
This needs symptom assessment but lacks the acute airway finding of stridor.
takeaway: New airway compromise takes priority over stable, routine needs.

title: A client declines care
stem: A capable adult declines a prescribed dressing change after the nurse explains its purpose. What is the best next action?
options: Ask the family to sign a refusal form before accepting the decision
Record the refusal and leave without exploring the reason or consequences
Explore the concern, respect the decision and communicate/document it
Return with another nurse to repeat the same explanation until the client agrees
why: A capable adult does not require family authorization to refuse.
Documentation alone misses an opportunity to address concerns and support informed refusal.
Clarify concerns without coercion, explain relevant consequences and communicate the informed refusal.
Repeating pressure for agreement risks coercion rather than supporting a voluntary choice.
takeaway: Consent is an ongoing conversation; a capable client may refuse.

title: Safe assignment
stem: Which task is the best candidate for assignment to a trained unregulated care provider, with clear instructions and supervision consistent with local policy?
options: Choose whether a client with new dizziness needs one-person or two-person transfer assistance
Help a stable client with an established bathing routine
Decide whether a stable client needs a prescribed as-needed laxative
Evaluate whether a client can safely use a newly prescribed walker without supervision
why: A new symptom requires nursing reassessment before assigning the assistance level.
A predictable personal-care task may be assigned after checking competence and client needs.
The decision requires assessment and medication-related judgment, not merely performance of a routine task.
Evaluating a new mobility aid and safety plan requires qualified assessment.
takeaway: Match client predictability, task, worker competence and supervision.

title: Need-to-know access
stem: A nurse notices a neighbour’s name in the electronic client list but is not involved in their care. What is appropriate?
options: Open only the admission summary because detailed notes are more private
Review the chart because employees are covered by the hospital confidentiality agreement
Ask a colleague caring for the neighbour to confirm the diagnosis
Do not access the record without a legitimate care-related purpose
why: Admission information is also protected personal health information.
An employment confidentiality agreement does not create a clinical need to access a record.
Personal curiosity does not authorize indirect access through a colleague.
Access is limited to an authorized purpose, not curiosity.
takeaway: Confidentiality includes appropriate access, not just avoiding disclosure.

title: An unfamiliar procedure
stem: A nurse is asked to perform a procedure they have never been trained to do. The client is stable. What is the best response?
options: Explain the competence gap and arrange a qualified practitioner or supervised learning plan
Use the written procedure because experience with a similar procedure should transfer
Ask a colleague for a brief demonstration and then perform the first attempt independently
Accept the assignment because a qualified colleague is available elsewhere on the unit
why: The stable situation permits a plan that provides competent care while addressing the nurse’s learning needs.
Related experience and written steps do not establish competence with the unfamiliar procedure.
A brief demonstration may support learning but does not establish readiness for an independent first attempt.
A colleague’s presence elsewhere does not by itself provide the planned supervision or competence needed.
takeaway: Authority, competence and the care context all matter.

title: A clear handover
stem: Which information belongs in a concise handover for a client with worsening shortness of breath? Select all that apply.
options: Current respiratory findings and vital-sign trends
Relevant history and interventions already given
A detailed account of stable baseline history before reporting the current respiratory deterioration
The specific assessment or assistance being requested
A diagnosis of pulmonary embolism stated as confirmed before diagnostic assessment
why: Current findings communicate urgency.
Relevant background and the response to care support clinical decisions.
Relevant baseline history matters, but lengthy stable background must not delay the urgent current findings and request.
A clear request closes the communication loop.
Communicate observed findings and concern; do not report an unconfirmed diagnosis as established.
takeaway: Structure handover around situation, background, assessment and recommendation.

title: An error in the record
stem: A nurse notices that they entered the wrong urine-output value in the electronic client record. What should the nurse do?
options: Replace the original entry with corrected text so only the accurate version remains
Use the approved correction process that preserves the audit trail
Write a new unrelated note with the correct number but do not identify the earlier error
Ask the next shift to make the correction under their own login
why: The correction process must preserve retrievable original information.
A transparent correction preserves the original entry and identifies the change.
A linked transparent correction is needed so readers can identify the erroneous information.
Accountability for the nurse’s entry should not be shifted to another login.
takeaway: Correct transparently; never conceal or falsify documentation.

title: Language and consent
stem: A client with limited English needs an explanation of a non-urgent invasive procedure. What is the best approach?
options: Use automated translation for the consent discussion and proceed if the client signs
Ask a visitor who speaks both languages to interpret the complete consent discussion
Arrange a qualified interpreter and confirm understanding
Give a translated form and treat the signature as sufficient confirmation
why: A nonurgent invasive-procedure consent discussion requires reliable communication and understanding, not reliance on an unverified automated translation.
A qualified interpreter is preferred for accuracy, confidentiality and complex consent when available.
Qualified interpretation supports accurate communication and meaningful consent.
Written material alone does not verify comprehension or answer individual questions.
takeaway: Assess understanding, not just apparent agreement.

title: A client safety concern
stem: An unregulated care provider reports that a usually alert client is suddenly confused. What should the nurse do first?
options: Ask the care provider to complete a confusion checklist before the nurse sees the client
Review previous cognitive assessments before checking the current vital signs
Call the family to determine baseline before attending the bedside
Assess the client promptly and escalate concerning findings
why: The report already warrants prompt direct assessment; a checklist must not postpone it.
Previous records can help later but do not take priority over assessment of an acute change.
Collateral information is useful but should not delay assessing the suddenly confused client.
Acute change requires assessment for causes such as hypoxia, infection or glucose disturbance.
takeaway: Treat new confusion as a change in condition, not normal aging.

title: Planning discharge
stem: A discharge prescription replaces the client’s previous antihypertensive. The client says, “I will take this one with the tablets I still have at home.” Which action best supports a safe transition?
options: Reconcile the medication list and ask the client to explain the plan back
Give both the old and new lists so the client can choose the familiar regimen
Explain the new prescription and ask the community pharmacy to resolve the old label later
Remove the discontinued medicine from the written list without asking what the client has at home
why: Reconciliation and teach-back help identify discrepancies and misunderstandings.
Conflicting regimens can cause duplication or omission.
The potentially conflicting directions should be reconciled before transition.
The client may still follow an older container label unless the change is clearly reconciled and understood.
takeaway: A safe handover includes what changed, how to take it and whom to contact.

title: Unsafe workload
stem: A nurse believes an assignment exceeds their ability to provide safe care. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Communicate specific risks promptly to the person responsible
Transfer the assignment to the next nurse without confirming that responsibility has been accepted
Request a revised assignment or additional qualified support
Follow the escalation process and document relevant communication
Record the concern only in a personal notebook without notifying the person responsible
why: Specific concerns allow risks to be addressed.
Continuity requires a clear transfer of responsibility, not an assumed handoff.
Adjusting workload or support can restore safe care.
Use organizational escalation and accurate documentation.
Private documentation alone does not enable timely resolution of the current safety risk.
takeaway: Escalate clearly and help preserve continuity of care.

title: Culturally safer care
stem: A client says previous experiences of discrimination make hospital care frightening. Which response is most therapeutic?
options: Our team has completed cultural-safety education, so you should feel safe here
Tell me what would help you feel safer while we plan your care
Let us finish the admission questions first and discuss past experiences later
I will ask someone from your community to choose the best approach for you
why: Training does not establish this client’s felt safety or address their individual concerns.
Invite the client’s perspective and collaborate on concrete needs.
Delaying the concern can overlook a current barrier to safe and trusting care.
Do not replace the client’s preferences with assumptions or another person’s choice.
takeaway: Ask, listen and share decisions rather than making cultural assumptions.

title: Hand hygiene
stem: After personal care, a nurse removes intact gloves. The hands are not visibly soiled and no organism-specific handwashing requirement applies. What should the nurse do next?
options: Put on new gloves before taking the same client’s oral temperature
Perform hand hygiene immediately after removing the gloves
Clean the hands after the remaining bedside tasks are finished
Disinfect the gloves before removing them and omit hand hygiene
why: Moving from personal care requires hand hygiene before further care and fresh gloves when indicated.
Glove removal can contaminate hands; visibly clean hands can generally be cleaned with alcohol-based hand rub unless another indication applies.
Deferring hygiene risks spreading contamination to subsequent tasks and surfaces.
Cleaning gloves does not substitute for removing them and cleaning the hands.
takeaway: Gloves are a barrier, not a substitute for hand hygiene.

title: Routine infection prevention
stem: Which actions support infection prevention? Select all that apply.
options: Clean hands before an aseptic task
Use a single-dose vial for two clients if each withdrawal uses a new sterile syringe
Select protective equipment for the anticipated exposure
Clean shared equipment between clients
Keep the same gloves when moving from perineal care to a clean dressing on the same client
why: Hand hygiene helps protect susceptible sites.
A new syringe does not make sharing a single-dose vial an appropriate routine practice.
Exposure risk determines the required protection.
Shared equipment can transmit organisms.
A move from a contaminated task to a clean/aseptic site requires glove removal, hand hygiene and appropriate new gloves.
takeaway: Protect each client with consistent routine practices.

title: A sharps injury
stem: A nurse sustains a used-needle puncture. After immediately washing the area, what is the priority?
options: Wait for the source client’s infection results before seeking exposure assessment
Complete the incident-report form before contacting occupational health
Promptly report and access the occupational exposure protocol
Ask a colleague whether the needle appeared bloody before deciding to report
why: Risk assessment and time-sensitive management should begin promptly.
Administrative reporting must not delay immediate clinical exposure assessment.
Prompt evaluation establishes the exposure risk and time-sensitive management.
A percutaneous used-needle exposure warrants prompt assessment even without visible blood.
takeaway: Treat occupational exposure as time-sensitive.

title: Preventing a fall
stem: An older adult becomes dizzy on standing after a new antihypertensive dose. What should the nurse do first?
options: Keep the client standing while obtaining an orthostatic blood pressure
Assist them to sit or lie safely and assess
Ask the client to hold the bedrail while the nurse retrieves a blood-pressure machine
Review the medication record before helping the client change position
why: Continuing unsupported standing can cause a fall when dizziness is already present.
Prevent the immediate fall, then assess symptoms and vital signs.
Stay and provide immediate physical safety or obtain assistance rather than leaving an unstable client.
The cause matters after the immediate fall risk is controlled.
takeaway: Stabilize the client before investigating the cause.

title: Airborne precautions
stem: A client is being assessed for infectious pulmonary tuberculosis. Which placement is most appropriate when available?
options: A private room with routine precautions while sputum results are pending
An airborne infection isolation room with the door closed
A private room under droplet precautions with a surgical mask for staff
A positive-pressure room used for protective isolation
why: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB requires airborne precautions before confirmation.
Airborne isolation and appropriate respiratory protection limit spread.
Pulmonary TB requires airborne rather than droplet respiratory protection and placement.
Positive pressure protects a susceptible occupant; it does not contain infectious airborne particles.
takeaway: Match the precautions to the suspected route of transmission.

title: A sterile field
stem: During sterile dressing setup, a nonsterile sleeve touches the centre of the sterile field. What should the nurse do?
options: Remove the items directly touched by the sleeve and use the remaining field
Place a sterile drape over the contact area and continue using the setup
Treat the field as contaminated and establish a new sterile field
Change gloves and continue with the original field
why: The sleeve touched the centre of the field, so removing selected items does not re-establish its sterility.
Covering the contact area does not reliably restore the contaminated sterile setup.
A breach requires replacement of the contaminated setup.
Changing gloves does not correct contamination of the field itself.
takeaway: If sterility is breached, replace rather than conceal.

title: Oxygen safety
stem: Which instructions are appropriate for a client using oxygen at home? Select all that apply.
options: Keep oxygen away from smoking and open flames
Increase the flow whenever breathlessness occurs, without using the prescribed action plan
Secure cylinders as instructed by the supplier
Follow the prescribed flow and equipment instructions
Store a spare cylinder upright beside the bed without securing it
why: Oxygen supports combustion and increases fire risk.
Oxygen flow should follow the prescription/action plan; worsening symptoms require assessment.
Securing cylinders reduces tipping and injury risk.
Use the prescribed settings and safe equipment procedures.
An unsecured cylinder can fall; store and secure it according to supplier instructions.
takeaway: Oxygen supports fire; protect the environment as well as the client.

title: Two identifiers
stem: Before administering a medication, which approach best verifies the client’s identity?
options: Compare the room number and the name on the door with the medication record
Compare the client’s full name with the same name printed on the medication cup
Compare two approved identifiers with the record and client identification
Ask whether the client is the name stated by the nurse and accept a nod
why: Room/location is not an approved personal identifier.
Repeating one identifier does not provide two independent approved identifiers.
Use the organization’s approved identifiers, such as name and date of birth.
A leading yes/no confirmation may produce an incorrect identity match.
takeaway: Verify identity each time required; do not rely on location or memory.

title: A clear walking route
stem: Which change is most useful for a client at risk of falling during night-time toileting?
options: Keep the walking aid at the doorway so the client will wait for help
Keep the route lit and clear, with the call bell and walking aid accessible
Rely on the bed-exit alarm without changing the dark, cluttered route
Remind the client to use the call bell but make no change to equipment placement
why: Placing a needed aid out of reach can increase unsafe reaching or unsupported movement.
Accessible assistance and a clear route reduce environmental hazards.
An alarm does not remove the environmental hazards.
Instructions alone do not address accessibility or the route hazard.
takeaway: Plan for the activity that is likely to happen, not only the bed space.

title: A damaged medication label
stem: The label on a prepared syringe is unreadable. What is the safest action?
options: Use the dose recorded in the medication administration record to infer the syringe contents
Ask the preparer to relabel it from memory without verifying its identity
Administer it after a second nurse confirms that its volume matches the prescription
Do not administer it; obtain a correctly identified preparation
why: The record does not independently establish what is in this syringe.
An unverifiable preparation should not be administered based only on recall.
Volume does not identify the medication or concentration.
The drug and dose must be verifiable before administration.
takeaway: An unidentified preparation is not safe to administer.

title: Medication storage
stem: A nurse finds two look-alike medication packages stored together after a near miss. What is the best response?
options: Report the near miss and work with the team to reduce selection risk
Move one package to an unlabelled drawer without involving pharmacy
Send a reminder to be more careful and close the near-miss review
Ask only the nurse involved to remember the package difference
why: Near-miss reporting can lead to safer storage, labels and checks.
An unapproved storage change may create a different selection risk.
A reminder alone leaves the look-alike storage hazard unchanged.
The hazard affects future users and requires a system response.
takeaway: Use near misses to improve the system.

title: A contaminated device
stem: A reusable blood-pressure cuff has been used for a client on additional precautions. What is the best action before use for another client?
options: Use the approved wipe and immediately dry the cuff with a towel
Follow the required cleaning/disinfection process and product contact time
Disinfect only if the previous client has a confirmed organism
Clean only the visible soil and use the cuff as soon as it looks dry
why: Drying prematurely may prevent the required disinfectant contact time.
Use the approved process appropriate to the device and exposure.
Routine equipment reprocessing is needed even when a specific organism is unconfirmed.
Visible cleaning alone may not complete the required disinfection process.
takeaway: Correct product, correct process, correct contact time.

title: Teach-back
stem: Which request best checks a client’s understanding of a new inhaler?
options: Ask the client to list the side effects of the inhaler
Please show me how you will use this inhaler at home
Ask the client how many years they have used inhalers
Ask the client to repeat the written steps without handling the device
why: Side-effect recall does not verify inhaler technique.
Demonstration reveals actual technique and allows supportive correction.
Prior exposure does not demonstrate correct use of this device.
Verbal recall alone can miss errors in timing or handling.
takeaway: Ask clients to demonstrate or explain in their own words.

title: Readiness to learn
stem: A client reports severe postoperative pain when the nurse begins discharge teaching. What is the best initial action?
options: Complete the essential teaching while arranging analgesia because discharge is scheduled
Teach the family alone and count the client’s teaching as complete
Address the pain and reassess readiness to learn
Give the prescribed analgesic and immediately resume all teaching without reassessment
why: Severe pain can undermine learning; symptom relief and reassessed readiness should guide timing.
Family support does not replace appropriate teaching and assessment of the client when they can participate.
Manage the immediate symptom so teaching can be effective.
Readiness, relief and possible sedation need reassessment before continuing.
takeaway: Address barriers before adding more information.

title: Infant sleep
stem: Which advice supports safer sleep for a healthy infant?
options: Place the infant on the side with a rolled towel to prevent rolling
Place the infant on the back on a firm, flat, separate sleep surface without loose bedding
Use a firm inclined sleep surface to reduce spit-up
Use a separate crib with a firm mattress and add a loose blanket for warmth
why: Side positioning and positioning aids do not provide the recommended safe sleep setup.
Back sleeping on a clear, firm, flat surface supports safer sleep.
Healthy infants should sleep on a flat surface; an incline is not the recommended routine solution for spit-up.
A clear sleep surface without loose bedding is safer; use appropriate sleep clothing.
takeaway: Use a clear, firm, flat sleep space and back positioning.

title: Preventing neural tube defects
stem: A client planning pregnancy asks why folic acid is discussed before conception. What is the best explanation?
options: It helps reduce neural tube defects during very early development
It is most useful once an ultrasound shows how the spine is developing
It mainly prevents the mother’s iron-deficiency anemia
It becomes necessary only after the first missed period
why: Neural tube development occurs early, often before pregnancy is recognized.
Neural tube development occurs before routine ultrasound can guide preventive timing.
Folic acid is not iron replacement; the specific preconception benefit tested is neural tube risk reduction.
Starting before conception matters because neural tube development occurs very early.
takeaway: Timing matters: preventive care can begin before pregnancy.

title: A vaccination concern
stem: A parent is worried about recommended childhood vaccines. Which response best supports informed decision-making?
options: Give a standard vaccine handout before asking what the parent has heard
Ask what worries them and discuss benefits and risks using current local guidance
Explain only the disease risk because adverse effects may increase worry
Recommend delaying the schedule until the parent no longer has questions
why: Begin by eliciting the specific concern so information is relevant and understandable.
Understand the concern and offer accurate, relevant information.
Balanced informed discussion includes relevant vaccine benefits and risks.
Unaddressed questions should prompt supportive discussion using current guidance, not automatic delay.
takeaway: Explore the concern before providing targeted education.

title: Diabetes foot care
stem: A client with diabetes and reduced protective sensation in both feet is reviewing home foot care. Which statements indicate appropriate understanding? Select all that apply.
options: I will inspect my feet daily
I will soak my feet for a long time each evening to soften the skin
I will check inside my shoes before wearing them
I will report a new blister or wound promptly
I will use a heating pad on low if my numb feet feel cold
why: Daily inspection may reveal injuries when sensation is reduced.
Prolonged soaking can damage/macerate skin; use the recommended cleaning and drying plan.
Small objects or rough areas may injure an insensate foot.
Early review can reduce complications.
Reduced sensation can prevent detection of a burn even at a low setting.
takeaway: Loss of protective sensation calls for daily protection and inspection.

title: Smoking cessation
stem: A client says, “I want to quit smoking, but I have failed before.” Which response is best?
options: Choose a quit date today before discussing why previous attempts ended
What helped before, and what made it difficult? We can plan support around that
Use exactly the same method again because it worked for a short time
Wait until you feel completely confident before seeking cessation support
why: A date may be helpful later; first understand the client’s experience and barriers.
Explore strengths and barriers, then discuss appropriate supports.
A prior attempt can inform care, but the plan should address why it was not sustained.
Support can help build confidence and address ambivalence now.
takeaway: Treat previous attempts as information for the next plan.

title: Accessible education
stem: A client has difficulty reading the discharge instructions. Which changes may help? Select all that apply.
options: Use plain language and short sections
Provide a longer written explanation of every step to cover the possible questions
Discuss the most important actions and use teach-back
Offer suitable pictures or demonstrations
Ask the client to sign the instructions as the main check of understanding
why: Clear language and manageable sections reduce the stated reading barrier.
More written content may increase burden without making the essential actions accessible.
Prioritizing and checking the client’s explanation tests usable understanding.
A suitable visual or practical approach can reduce reliance on difficult written material.
A signature does not demonstrate that the client can follow the plan.
takeaway: Adapt the explanation while preserving autonomy.

title: An older adult’s hearing
stem: An older adult with hearing difficulty is learning wound care. What should the nurse do?
options: Speak very slowly and exaggerate every lip movement
Increase volume until the client stops asking questions
Reduce background noise, face the client and check preferred communication supports
Ask a relative to repeat all information without checking the client’s preferred supports
why: Exaggerated speech can distort visual and auditory cues; normal clear speech and individual supports are preferable.
Volume alone does not address communication preference, background noise or understanding.
Optimize the environment and individual supports.
The client should guide communication supports and remain directly involved.
takeaway: Make communication accessible before judging comprehension.

title: Hydration during illness
stem: A caregiver asks about a child with diarrhea. Which finding requires prompt clinical assessment?
options: Three loose stools in a day while the child is alert and passing urine as usual
Marked lethargy with very little urine
Reduced appetite while the child drinks oral rehydration fluid and remains interactive
A mild thirst that improves after drinking, with usual wet diapers
why: This warrants advice/monitoring but is less urgent than lethargy with very low urine output.
Reduced urine and marked lethargy may indicate significant dehydration or illness.
Preserved drinking and interaction are more reassuring than marked lethargy and oliguria.
This is less concerning than persistent lethargy with low output.
takeaway: Assess the whole child, including behaviour and urine output.

title: A new breast change
stem: An adult reports a new persistent breast lump. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Book the next routine screening mammogram and reassess after it
Arrange timely clinical assessment rather than waiting for routine screening
Monitor it for several more months because the recent screen was normal
Seek assessment only if pain or nipple discharge develops
why: A persistent new symptom needs timely diagnostic assessment rather than a screening pathway alone.
New symptoms need diagnostic assessment, independently of a screening schedule.
A recent normal screen does not exclude a new or missed symptomatic problem.
A persistent lump itself warrants assessment even without additional symptoms.
takeaway: Screening is for asymptomatic populations; new symptoms need assessment.

title: Prenatal warning signs
stem: A client at 32 weeks of pregnancy reports a new severe headache, visual changes and upper abdominal pain. What is the most appropriate advice?
options: Record the symptoms and discuss them at tomorrow’s scheduled prenatal visit
Arrange urgent maternity assessment
Rest in a dark room and seek assessment only if the headache remains after several hours
Check blood pressure at a pharmacy later today before deciding whether to call maternity triage
why: This symptom combination warrants urgent assessment rather than waiting for a routine appointment.
Urgent assessment is needed for possible pre-eclampsia or another acute problem.
Home observation may delay evaluation of a serious obstetric complication.
Symptoms themselves justify urgent maternity assessment; a preliminary community reading should not delay it.
takeaway: Recognize warning symptoms and escalate without diagnosing from one symptom.

title: Therapeutic silence
stem: A client begins to cry after receiving difficult news. What is the best initial response?
options: Stay present and invite them to share what they are feeling
Tell the client about another person who recovered from the same problem
Begin explaining all available treatment options while the client is crying
Say that staying positive will help treatment work
why: Presence and an open invitation support expression without pressure.
Another person’s experience may redirect attention away from this client’s feelings.
Information may be useful later; first offer presence and assess readiness.
This can pressure the client to suppress understandable feelings.
takeaway: Support expression before trying to solve the emotion.

title: Assessing suicide risk
stem: A client says, “There is no point in living.” What is the best response?
options: Ask what happened today and explore the social stressor before asking about suicide
Ask directly about suicidal thoughts, intent, plan and access to means
Ask whether the client has supportive relatives and assume that support makes them safe
Reassure the client that these feelings often improve and offer a follow-up visit
why: Explore stressors, but do not postpone direct assessment of the potential suicide risk.
Direct assessment helps determine immediate safety needs and escalation.
Protective factors do not exclude suicidal intent or access to means.
Reassurance and later follow-up do not replace immediate risk assessment.
takeaway: Ask directly and respond to risk with appropriate safety support.

title: Responding to hallucinations
stem: A client says a voice is ordering them to hurt someone. Which response is the priority?
options: Ask the client to describe when the voices began before exploring the threat
Offer distraction and reassess whether the voice is present at the next check
Assess the command, intent and immediate risk, and seek appropriate help
Explain that staff do not hear the voice and continue the usual care plan
why: History is useful, but content, intent and immediate safety take priority.
Distraction alone does not establish safety after a command to harm.
Potential commands to harm require prompt risk assessment and protective action.
Reality-based communication should be combined with a direct assessment of risk.
takeaway: Assess the content and safety implications without endorsing the hallucination.

title: Acute panic
stem: A client is acutely anxious, breathing rapidly and unable to follow long instructions. What is most helpful initially?
options: Start a detailed relaxation teaching session and ask the client to memorize the steps
Stay with the client, use short calm statements and assess physical safety
Ask the client to breathe into a paper bag before checking oxygenation or other physical causes
Ask the client to identify the cause of every previous anxiety episode
why: Lengthy teaching is poorly matched to the current inability to process instructions.
A calm presence and simple communication support safety and regulation.
This can be unsafe when a medical cause of tachypnea has not been assessed.
Detailed retrospective exploration can wait until the acute distress and physical safety are addressed.
takeaway: Match the amount of information to the client’s current ability to process it.

title: Supporting a grieving client
stem: Which response is most appropriate to “I should be over this loss by now”?
options: It is normal to grieve for a year, so no further assessment is needed yet
You should put away reminders of the person so the feelings happen less often
There is no single timetable. How is this affecting your daily life?
If you stay busy enough, you will notice the grief less
why: A timetable should not replace assessment of function, support and safety.
This imposes a coping approach without exploring the client’s needs.
Acknowledge variation and assess functioning, support and safety.
Activity may help some people but does not replace individualized assessment or support.
takeaway: Individualize support and assess impact rather than imposing a timetable.

title: Responding to a delusion
stem: A client appears frightened and says, “The television is sending secret instructions only to me.” Which response is best?
options: Let us compare the secret messages you receive with the ones I receive
The television cannot send private messages; let us review how broadcasting works
I do not receive those messages, but I can see this is distressing for you
We will turn off the television, and then you will no longer receive messages
why: This endorses the premise of secret messages instead of maintaining a reality-based, supportive response.
A technical argument is unlikely to reduce distress or build trust.
State your reality while acknowledging the emotion.
This response endorses the proposed source of the messages rather than acknowledging distress without agreement.
takeaway: Validate the feeling, not the false belief.

title: De-escalation
stem: Which actions may help when a client is becoming verbally agitated but has not assaulted anyone? Select all that apply.
options: Use a calm tone and simple choices
Stand close enough to prevent the client from walking away during the discussion
Maintain appropriate personal space
Reduce unnecessary stimulation and call for support as needed
Have several staff give instructions together so the message is reinforced
why: Calm, clear choices can support a sense of control.
Crowding or blocking exit can increase perceived threat and escalation.
Personal space helps reduce perceived threat.
A safer environment and timely support can prevent escalation.
Multiple simultaneous directions increase stimulation and can feel threatening.
takeaway: De-escalation combines respect, space and safety planning.

title: Alcohol withdrawal
stem: A hospitalized client who abruptly stopped heavy alcohol use develops tremor, sweating and agitation. What should the nurse do?
options: Treat the symptoms as anxiety unless the client reports a previous withdrawal seizure
Assess promptly and escalate for withdrawal management under protocol
Reduce stimulation and wait for the next routine observations before using a withdrawal tool
Complete a full long-term alcohol history before reporting the current autonomic symptoms
why: Withdrawal can occur without a known previous seizure and requires assessment.
Withdrawal can progress to seizures or delirium and needs timely management.
A quiet environment can help but does not replace prompt assessment and escalation.
History must not delay timely evaluation and management of evolving withdrawal.
takeaway: Substance withdrawal can be an acute physiological emergency.

title: Trauma-informed care
stem: Which actions support trauma-informed care during a physical assessment? Select all that apply.
options: Explain each step and ask permission before touch
Treat the signed admission consent as permission to continue if the client asks to pause
Offer reasonable choices and a way to pause
Protect privacy and ask about preferences
Ask for a detailed trauma narrative before offering a less exposing examination position
why: Predictability and permission support safety.
Consent is ongoing; a request to pause needs acknowledgement and reassessment.
Choice and a pause signal support autonomy.
Privacy and preferences help build trust.
Safety, choice and practical accommodations need not depend on trauma disclosure.
takeaway: Create safety and choice without requiring a trauma history.

title: Dementia and distress
stem: A client with dementia repeatedly asks to go home. What is a helpful response?
options: Repeat the hospital address until the client can say it correctly
Acknowledge the wish and explore comfort or familiar routines
Show the client the chart note stating that they cannot return home
Tell the client that they can go home after supper even though no discharge is planned
why: Repeated correction may increase distress without addressing the need behind the request.
Address the emotion and possible unmet needs.
A record-based argument is unlikely to address the emotional need.
A false promise can undermine trust and may lead to further distress.
takeaway: Look for the need behind the repeated request.

title: Professional boundaries
stem: A client offers the nurse an expensive personal gift in return for extra attention. What is the best response?
options: Accept the gift if the same amount of nursing attention is maintained
Accept the gift after documenting that the client offered it voluntarily
Respectfully decline or redirect the expensive gift, explore the concern and explain that care is based on need
Hold the gift until discharge and accept it after the client leaves
why: An expensive personal gift still creates a significant boundary concern.
Voluntariness and documentation do not remove the professional power imbalance or significant-gift restriction.
A significant gift contingent on extra attention should not be accepted; preserve the therapeutic relationship and follow regulator/employer guidance.
Waiting until discharge does not automatically resolve a boundary concern arising from the care relationship.
takeaway: Warmth and professional boundaries are compatible.

title: Possible intimate-partner violence
stem: A client’s partner answers every question and refuses to leave. The client seems fearful. What should the nurse arrange when safe?
options: A private conversation with the client using a safe, routine approach
Ask the partner in front of the client whether controlling behaviour occurs at home
Send written abuse-service information home in a bag the partner will carry
Ask the partner to describe the client’s concerns while the client completes paperwork
why: Privacy supports assessment, choice and safety planning.
A direct confrontation may increase danger and inhibit disclosure.
Visible materials may expose help-seeking and should be offered through a safe individualized plan.
This preserves the partner’s control of communication instead of giving the client a safe private opportunity.
takeaway: Create a safe opportunity to talk privately before making assumptions.

title: Swallowing difficulty
stem: A client coughs repeatedly and develops a wet voice while drinking after a stroke. What should the nurse do first?
options: Switch to thickened liquid and finish the drink before contacting the swallowing team
Stop oral intake and seek assessment according to the swallowing protocol
Offer smaller sips through a straw and reassess after the meal
Continue with food but omit liquids until the next scheduled review
why: Do not independently continue oral intake after new unsafe-swallowing signs without assessment and a plan.
Stop the exposure and obtain an appropriate swallowing assessment.
A straw or smaller volume does not establish safe swallowing.
Swallowing risk may affect food and medicines too; stop oral intake and arrange assessment.
takeaway: New signs of swallowing difficulty require reassessment before more intake.

title: Pressure injury prevention
stem: An immobile client is incontinent and eats less than half of meals. Which measures belong in an individualized pressure-injury prevention plan? Select all that apply.
options: Inspect skin and reassess risk
Massage the reddened sacrum at each turn to improve circulation
Individualize repositioning and offload heels
Address moisture and nutritional needs
Use the pressure-redistributing mattress as the reason to omit individualized repositioning
why: Inspection detects changes and helps tailor the plan.
Massage over pressure-damaged tissue can worsen injury.
Reducing prolonged pressure is a central preventive measure.
Moisture and nutrition affect skin integrity.
Support surfaces supplement skin assessment and individualized pressure relief; they do not replace them.
takeaway: Use an individualized bundle rather than relying on one device.

title: Supporting independence
stem: A client can wash their face and upper body but needs help with the legs. What is the best approach?
options: Complete the bath for the client each morning to conserve all their energy
Encourage the client’s abilities and assist where needed
Set out supplies and leave the client to complete the lower-body care unaided
Ask the family to take over all personal care until the client can wash independently
why: This removes abilities the client can safely exercise rather than balancing support and independence.
Match assistance to ability and preferences.
The assessed difficulty with the legs requires assistance.
Family involvement may help, but all-or-nothing assistance needlessly removes retained ability.
takeaway: Help enough to make care safe while preserving what the client can do.

title: Pain assessment
stem: An alert client reports pain of 8/10 while appearing calm. What should guide the assessment?
options: Record a lower score because facial expression and conversation are unchanged
Use the client’s report and assess location, character, function and associated findings
Use a behavioural pain scale instead of asking further questions
Confirm the expected pain score for the procedure before accepting the client’s rating
why: Observed behaviour cannot invalidate a communicative client’s pain report.
Self-report is central when the client can communicate; assess the broader context.
Behavioural tools do not replace self-report when the client can communicate.
Expected patterns are context, not a substitute for this client’s report and assessment.
takeaway: A calm appearance does not invalidate reported pain.

title: Evaluating comfort
stem: After an ordered analgesic and repositioning, what is the most useful next step?
options: Ask only whether the client is satisfied with care
Reassess pain, function and adverse effects at an appropriate interval
Wait until the next dose is due before checking the response
Recheck the pain number without assessing sedation, breathing or function
why: Satisfaction alone does not assess pain relief, function or adverse effects.
Evaluate both relief and safety, considering route and expected onset.
Reassessment should match route/onset and clinical condition, not merely the next dosing time.
Response and adverse effects both need assessment; a pain score alone is incomplete.
takeaway: An intervention is incomplete until its effect is evaluated.

title: Preventing constipation
stem: Which plan best supports bowel function in a stable client without fluid or dietary restrictions?
options: Rely on a daily laxative while leaving fluid intake and mobility unassessed
Use regular toileting opportunities, suitable fluids, fibre and activity
Increase fibre rapidly without reviewing whether fluid intake is adequate
Schedule toileting only when staff have time rather than when the client reports an urge
why: An assessed plan addresses modifiable factors and uses medicines appropriately.
Multiple modifiable factors can support bowel regularity.
Fibre advice should be suitable and considered together with hydration and tolerance.
Regular opportunities and responding to the urge support bowel function.
takeaway: Tailor bowel care to the person and any restrictions.

title: A urinary drainage system
stem: Which actions help maintain a safely functioning indwelling urinary drainage system? Select all that apply.
options: Keep the bag below bladder level without resting it on the floor
Disconnect the bag every shift to empty residual urine from the tubing
Prevent dependent loops and kinks that obstruct flow
Maintain the closed system unless a clinical indication requires change
Clamp the tubing routinely during transfers so the bag can rest on the mattress
why: This supports drainage and reduces contamination risk.
Unnecessary disconnection breaches the closed drainage system.
Unobstructed flow helps avoid urinary stasis.
Preserve the closed system under the care protocol.
Routine clamping and elevating the bag can obstruct drainage or promote backflow; follow the transfer plan while keeping drainage dependent.
takeaway: Preserve closed, unobstructed dependent drainage.

title: A safe transfer
stem: A client cannot bear weight reliably. What is the safest plan for moving them from bed to chair?
options: Use a two-person underarm lift because it avoids waiting for equipment
Use the assessed transfer plan and appropriate lift with trained assistance
Use a standing transfer aid without reassessing the client’s ability to bear weight
Apply a transfer belt and repeat yesterday’s pivot transfer with one nurse
why: Additional people do not make an inappropriate manual lift safe.
Match equipment and assistance to assessed ability and policy.
A standing aid requires suitable assessed ability; unreliable weight bearing may require a different lift.
An established method should not be repeated when current ability does not support it.
takeaway: Choose transfer support from ability, not from staff strength.

title: Improving sleep
stem: A stable inpatient reports being awakened repeatedly by avoidable noise and separate nonurgent care visits. Necessary overnight monitoring must continue. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Cluster suitable care activities and reduce avoidable noise and light
Request a bedtime sedative before trying the agreed environmental changes
Delay all overnight observations until morning so sleep is uninterrupted
Move all personal care to late evening even if the client prefers an earlier bedtime
why: Reducing avoidable disruption supports rest while maintaining necessary monitoring.
When avoidable disruption is identified, modify it and evaluate the effect before assuming medicine is needed.
Necessary monitoring cannot be omitted merely to promote sleep.
Care clustering should be suitable for the clinical needs and client preferences.
takeaway: Reduce modifiable disruptions without omitting necessary monitoring.

title: Oral care and aspiration risk
stem: A dependent client with reduced alertness needs oral hygiene. What is most appropriate?
options: Clean with a wet swab while the client lies flat because the head cannot be held upright
Use an assessed positioning and suction-assisted oral-care approach under protocol
Use only lip moisturizer until normal alertness returns
Use a large volume of mouth rinse because suction is available
why: Position must support drainage and airway safety; lying flat with fluid may increase aspiration risk.
Adapt oral care to airway protection and swallowing ability.
The mouth still needs appropriate gentle cleaning, not lip care alone.
Suction availability does not justify unnecessary oral fluid or loss of airway precautions.
takeaway: Modify the technique to the client’s airway and swallowing risk.

title: Nutrition support
stem: An older client has poor appetite and becomes fatigued during meals. Which plan is most appropriate?
options: Schedule the main meal immediately after bathing and physiotherapy to keep care activities together
Assess causes and offer small, suitable nutrient-dense meals with assistance as needed
Record low intake as the client’s usual pattern and reassess at the next weekly weight
Remove snacks between meals to increase appetite at the next main meal
why: Clustering exertional care immediately before eating may worsen known meal fatigue; assess and plan rest and assistance around meals.
Assess symptoms, swallowing, dental issues and support needs; individualize the plan.
Poor intake and fatigue need assessment and an individualized plan now.
This can reduce total intake in someone who fatigues during larger meals.
takeaway: Low intake is an assessment cue, not an inevitable feature of aging.

title: Comfort at end of life
stem: A dying client has a dry mouth but cannot safely swallow. What is the most appropriate comfort measure?
options: Give frequent spoonfuls of water to reach the usual oral fluid target
Provide frequent gentle mouth care and lip moisture using appropriate products
Offer ice chips without reassessing swallowing because they melt slowly
Request intravenous fluid solely to replace bedside mouth care
why: Unsafe swallowing makes forced oral water a risk of aspiration and distress.
Mouth care can relieve dryness without forcing unsafe intake.
Melting ice still becomes oral fluid; do not assume swallowing safety when it is known to be impaired.
Hydration decisions are individualized; they do not replace direct mouth care for comfort.
takeaway: Comfort-focused care continues even when oral intake is unsafe.

title: Medication reconciliation
stem: A client’s home medication list differs from the admission orders. What should the nurse do?
options: Use the admission list because every discrepancy must be intentional
Clarify and reconcile discrepancies with the appropriate team before uncertain doses
Use the home list because it is the most familiar regimen to the client
Leave the discrepancy for discharge reconciliation and give the uncertain dose now
why: Discrepancies require clarification rather than an assumption.
Determine what is intended and resolve discrepancies.
Home information is important but does not establish the intended inpatient prescription.
An uncertain current dose needs resolution before administration.
takeaway: Resolve discrepancies rather than guessing the intended regimen.

title: Insulin and a delayed meal
stem: A client’s meal is unexpectedly delayed just before a scheduled rapid-acting mealtime insulin dose. What should the nurse do?
options: Give the mealtime dose now because the glucose is above target, without confirming carbohydrate availability
Check glucose and coordinate the dose with meal availability and the prescribed plan
Withhold the entire day’s insulin plan because one meal is delayed
Reduce the mealtime dose by half without checking the prescription or protocol
why: Meal and correction components must follow the prescribed plan and actual food availability.
Assess glucose and clarify timing under the order/protocol rather than making an unsupported change.
Basal and other insulin needs may remain; do not cancel all therapy based on one meal delay.
An unsupported dose change is not a substitute for glucose assessment and plan coordination.
takeaway: Link mealtime insulin timing to the actual meal and prescribed regimen.

title: Warfarin teaching
stem: Which statement by a client taking warfarin indicates appropriate understanding?
options: I will avoid leafy green vegetables so my INR stays stable
I will keep vitamin K intake reasonably consistent and attend INR monitoring
Once my INR is stable, dietary changes will no longer affect the dose
I will adjust my dose whenever I eat more vitamin K than usual
why: Complete avoidance is generally unnecessary; consistent intake is the teaching priority.
Diet changes and INR results affect management; follow the prescribed plan.
Diet and interacting products can still alter anticoagulation after an initially stable INR.
Dose changes should follow the anticoagulation plan, not unsupervised adjustments.
takeaway: Think consistency, interaction checks and monitoring.

title: Opioid-related deterioration
stem: After an opioid dose, a client is difficult to arouse with slow, shallow respirations. What is the priority?
options: Apply oxygen and reassess at the next observations without calling for help
Withhold further opioid, call for urgent help and support airway/breathing; follow reversal protocol
Check the pain score before deciding whether a reversal protocol is needed
Wait for the opioid to wear off while withholding the next scheduled dose
why: Oxygen alone does not correct opioid-related hypoventilation or replace urgent assessment.
Support ventilation and activate emergency care; give reversal treatment as authorized.
Difficulty arousing and slow shallow breathing demand immediate airway/ventilation support.
Withholding a future dose alone does not treat present respiratory depression.
takeaway: Respiratory depression requires immediate action, not routine reassessment later.

title: A potassium order
stem: A nurse receives an order for concentrated potassium chloride by direct IV push. What should happen?
options: Administer it by IV push using a slower rate than the order specifies
Clarify the unsafe order and do not give direct IV push potassium
Dilute it in a small flush syringe and give it through a running IV
Ask a second nurse to check it and proceed if the serum potassium is low
why: A slower direct push does not make concentrated potassium safe.
Potassium requires an appropriate diluted infusion under controlled administration policy.
Small-volume push dilution is not an approved controlled potassium infusion.
An independent check and indication cannot legitimize an unsafe route.
takeaway: The need for replacement never makes direct IV push potassium safe.

title: A suspected medication reaction
stem: Soon after an IV antibiotic begins, a client develops wheezing, facial swelling and hypotension. The infusion has been stopped and emergency help summoned. Which medicine should the nurse give first under the authorized anaphylaxis protocol?
options: The protocol antihistamine for the facial swelling
Intramuscular epinephrine for the systemic reaction
The protocol inhaled bronchodilator for wheezing
The protocol corticosteroid for the allergic response
why: An antihistamine does not treat life-threatening airway swelling or shock and should not delay epinephrine.
Prompt IM epinephrine is first-line treatment for anaphylaxis; continue airway/circulatory support and emergency care.
A bronchodilator may be an adjunct for bronchospasm but does not replace epinephrine for multisystem anaphylaxis.
Corticosteroids do not provide the rapid first-line reversal needed for this acute respiratory and circulatory reaction.
takeaway: Anaphylaxis is an airway and circulation emergency.

title: Checking a medication order
stem: Which findings require clarification before administration? Select all that apply.
options: The dose is missing
A documented allergy conflicts with the prescribed medication
The prescription is complete and the client’s name and birth date match the administration record
The route is unclear
The ordered dose is available in a verified concentration and the calculated volume has been checked
why: A dose must be clear and appropriate.
Clarify the allergy and treatment plan before exposing the client.
These completed checks do not themselves require clarification.
The intended route must be unambiguous.
Verified dose/concentration information is not an unresolved discrepancy.
takeaway: Clarify omissions, ambiguity and relevant contraindications.

title: IV infiltration
stem: A peripheral IV site becomes cool, swollen and painful while a non-vesicant fluid is infusing. What should the nurse do first?
options: Lower the infusion rate and reassess whether the swelling spreads
Stop the infusion and assess/manage the site under protocol
Flush the cannula to distinguish infiltration from a blocked line
Check the pump history before stopping because no alarm has sounded
why: Further infusion may worsen infiltration; stopping is the first action.
Stop further fluid entry and assess the suspected infiltration.
Flushing can introduce more fluid into tissue and should not precede stopping and assessment.
Pump alarms do not reliably detect infiltration and should not delay stopping the infusion.
takeaway: Assess the client and site; do not depend on the pump alarm.

title: Safe abbreviations
stem: A prescribed dose is one-half milligram. Which notation follows safer medication-writing conventions?
options: .5 mg
0.5 mg
.50 mg
why: Omitting the leading zero can lead to a decimal being missed.
Use a leading zero before a decimal and avoid unnecessary trailing zeros.
An unnecessary trailing zero can be misread if the decimal is missed.
This combines a missing leading zero with an unnecessary trailing zero.
takeaway: Use a leading zero; avoid unnecessary trailing zeros.

title: Extended-release tablets
stem: A client with swallowing difficulty has an extended-release tablet prescribed. What is the best action?
options: Crush the tablet because the dose will remain the same
Ask the pharmacist/prescriber about a suitable alternative or approved administration method
Split the tablet because all extended-release products can be split
Substitute another brand with the same milligram strength without checking its release properties
why: Crushing an extended-release product can alter release and exposure even when the total milligrams are unchanged.
Verify formulation-specific handling and arrange an appropriate option.
Splitting is product-specific; it cannot be assumed safe for all extended-release tablets.
The same stated strength does not establish equivalent release or safe alteration; verify the exact formulation and authorized alternative.
takeaway: The dosage form matters as much as the drug name.

title: Checking after a diuretic
stem: A client taking a loop diuretic reports weakness and palpitations. Which prescribed laboratory test is particularly relevant to review promptly?
options: Serum potassium
Serum sodium
Serum creatinine
Hemoglobin
why: Loop-diuretic potassium loss can directly contribute to both weakness and dysrhythmia, making this a priority result alongside clinical assessment.
Sodium is relevant to fluid/electrolyte assessment but is less directly linked than potassium to the new palpitation pattern.
Renal function helps evaluate treatment tolerance, but potassium more directly addresses a potential electrolyte-related rhythm problem.
Anaemia can cause weakness and palpitations, but the loop-diuretic exposure specifically raises concern for potassium depletion.
takeaway: Connect medication effects with new symptoms and monitoring.

title: Medication teaching
stem: Which instructions support safe use of a new medicine at home? Select all that apply.
options: Explain its purpose and prescribed schedule
Explain important adverse effects and when to seek help
Give all instructions at once and use the client’s signature as the only understanding check
Check for understanding and relevant nonprescription products
Review prescribed medicines only because over-the-counter products do not appear on the prescription
why: Purpose and timing support appropriate use.
The client needs clear instructions about concerning effects.
A signature does not demonstrate usable understanding; tailor teaching and use teach-back.
Teach-back and interaction review identify safety issues.
Nonprescription medicines and supplements can interact and need review.
takeaway: Teach the purpose, practical use, monitoring and escalation plan.

title: A trend in deterioration
stem: A postoperative client’s observations are shown below. What is the best response?
options: Repeat the observations in one hour because postoperative tachycardia is common
Assess promptly and escalate possible bleeding or circulatory deterioration
Treat the lower urine output as catheter obstruction and review the circulation later
Document an expected response to analgesia without assessing the client
why: Hypotension plus tachycardia and oliguria needs immediate assessment and escalation.
Falling pressure with rising pulse and reduced urine suggests compromised perfusion.
Catheter function may be checked, but the full pattern suggests impaired perfusion and cannot be reduced to a drainage issue.
A medication explanation cannot be assumed for these concerning trends.
takeaway: Interpret the pattern, not a single reassuring value.

title: Critical potassium
stem: A client’s potassium result is 6.4 mmol/L (reference 3.5–5.0 mmol/L). What should the nurse do?
options: Repeat the sample and await confirmation before requesting a cardiac assessment
Assess, notify the clinician and arrange urgent ECG and monitoring as indicated
Review potassium intake and the next supplement dose before deciding on urgency
Obtain routine observations and use the next scheduled sample to evaluate the trend
why: Possible pseudohyperkalaemia can be investigated while prompt assessment and notification proceed; it must not delay care.
A potassium of 6.4 mmol/L needs urgent assessment and ECG; ongoing monitoring depends on the clinical findings, trend and protocol.
Medication and intake review may contribute to management but do not replace urgent assessment of this value.
Routine delayed follow-up is inadequate for a potentially dangerous potassium elevation.
takeaway: Potentially dangerous laboratory results require timely escalation.

title: After a fall
stem: A client is found on the floor after an unwitnessed fall. What should happen before routinely lifting the client?
options: Assess responsiveness, immediate threats and possible injury, and summon help
Transfer to bed with a mechanical lift so a full assessment can be completed comfortably
Check whether the client can stand before deciding if an injury assessment is needed
Review the medication record and complete fall-risk documentation before attending to injury
why: Assess injury and immediate danger before selecting a safe transfer method.
Routine movement should follow initial assessment of threats and possible injury, unless immediate environmental danger requires movement.
Ability to stand does not exclude injury and an unassessed attempt may cause harm.
Immediate clinical assessment takes precedence over investigation and documentation.
takeaway: Assess first unless the environment creates an immediate danger requiring movement.

title: Postoperative prevention
stem: Which actions can help reduce postoperative complications when appropriate to the client and care plan? Select all that apply.
options: Encourage prescribed deep breathing and supported coughing
Assist early mobilization when safe
Keep the client in bed until all postoperative pain has resolved
Assess pain and support adequate analgesia
Omit coughing and deep breathing because they increase incisional discomfort
why: These measures can support lung expansion and secretion clearance.
Movement helps reduce risks associated with immobility.
Safe early mobilization can occur with assessed pain control; zero pain is not a universal prerequisite.
Pain control can improve breathing and mobility.
Treat pain and support prescribed respiratory activities rather than omitting them without assessment.
takeaway: Support breathing and mobility while monitoring new symptoms.

title: A changing cast assessment
stem: A client with a new lower-leg cast reports worsening pain despite analgesia and numb toes. What is the priority?
options: Elevate the limb and wait to see whether the next analgesic dose resolves the symptoms
Assess neurovascular status and seek urgent review
Apply cold to the cast and reassess at the next routine observations
Loosen the outer bedding and continue routine cast care because toe numbness is expected
why: Comfort measures should not delay urgent review of worsening pain with sensory change.
Prompt neurovascular assessment and escalation protect the limb.
Symptom treatment alone does not address possible acute neurovascular compromise.
New numbness with worsening pain is a warning finding and not an expected routine response.
takeaway: Pain out of proportion and new sensory changes are warning findings.

title: Before a procedure
stem: A client scheduled for a non-urgent procedure says, “I signed, but I do not know what they are going to do.” What should the nurse do?
options: Confirm that the form is signed and continue because the clinician obtained consent
Pause preparation and arrange clarification of understanding and consent with the appropriate clinician
Give the preprocedure sedative first so the client can discuss concerns calmly
Read the procedure name from the form and ask the client to initial it again
why: A new expressed lack of understanding warrants clarification despite a signature.
Resolve the concern before proceeding with an elective procedure.
Sedation should not precede resolution of a nonurgent informed-consent concern.
Repeating paperwork does not establish meaningful understanding.
takeaway: Unresolved understanding requires clarification, even after signing.

title: Anticoagulation and a head injury
stem: A client taking an anticoagulant reports hitting their head and now has a worsening headache. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Arrange an INR and decide on assessment after the result returns
Arrange urgent clinical assessment
Advise omitting the next dose and arrange a routine review tomorrow
Monitor at home unless external bruising or loss of consciousness develops
why: A worsening headache after head injury requires urgent assessment; INR does not exclude traumatic bleeding.
Head injury with anticoagulation and new symptoms requires urgent assessment.
A dose omission does not assess or treat possible intracranial bleeding.
Serious intracranial bleeding can occur without these findings.
takeaway: Internal bleeding may not be visible.

title: Monitoring fluid status
stem: Which findings support a new increase in fluid volume when considered with the full clinical assessment? Select all that apply.
options: A rapid increase in weight measured on the same scale under consistent conditions
New breathlessness with bilateral crackles
Dry mucous membranes with falling weight and reduced intake
Increasing peripheral edema with a progressively positive intake/output balance
Postural dizziness with a negative fluid balance after ongoing gastrointestinal losses
why: An acute, consistently measured weight gain can support increasing fluid volume.
New breathlessness and crackles can reflect pulmonary congestion and need assessment.
This cluster more strongly suggests fluid loss or insufficient intake than a new increase in volume.
These trends can support fluid accumulation when considered with the broader assessment.
This pattern supports possible volume depletion, not new fluid accumulation.
takeaway: Use several converging findings to assess a fluid trend.

title: A wound change
stem: A postoperative wound develops spreading redness, warmth, increasing pain and purulent drainage. What is appropriate?
options: Change the dressing and wait for the next routine surgical review before reporting
Assess the client including systemic signs and report possible infection
Swab the drainage and wait for culture results before reporting the change
Apply a larger absorbent dressing and assess only the surrounding skin
why: Spreading inflammatory signs and purulent drainage require prompt assessment and communication.
Assess locally and systemically and communicate for timely management.
Testing may be ordered, but clinical assessment/reporting should not wait for culture.
Dressing selection does not replace assessment for systemic illness and escalation.
takeaway: Look beyond the wound for signs of systemic illness.

title: A transfusion reaction
stem: Shortly after a blood transfusion starts, a client develops chills, back pain and dyspnea. What is the priority?
options: Slow the transfusion and give prescribed acetaminophen before reporting
Stop the transfusion and activate the transfusion-reaction protocol with urgent assessment
Check the compatibility label while allowing the transfusion to continue
Give oxygen and reassess after ten minutes before deciding whether to stop the unit
why: Potential serious transfusion reaction requires stopping exposure rather than merely slowing it.
Stop the suspected exposure, assess urgently and follow protocol for access, notification and investigation.
Identity/clerical checks are important but must not delay stopping a suspected reaction.
Supportive oxygen does not replace prompt cessation and urgent reaction management.
takeaway: Stop a suspected transfusion reaction promptly and follow the emergency protocol.

title: An acute neurological change
stem: A client suddenly develops facial asymmetry and arm weakness. Which information is especially important to determine while urgent help is activated?
options: The last time the client was known to be at their usual neurological baseline
The exact time the nurse first documented the abnormal findings
The time the client last ate a meal
The time the last routine medication was administered
why: Last-known-well time informs time-sensitive stroke assessment and treatment options.
Recognition/documentation time may differ from the last time known at baseline.
This is not the time anchor used for acute stroke eligibility decisions.
Medication history matters, but last-known-well is the critical neurological time anchor asked for.
takeaway: Activate urgent care and establish last known well without delaying help.

title: Pulse oximeter limitations
stem: A pulse oximeter reads 82% on a cold finger, but the client is alert and speaking comfortably. What is best?
options: Warm the hand and repeat the reading at the next routine observation round
Apply prescribed oxygen and judge response from whether the client appears more comfortable
Assess immediately and verify a reliable signal while arranging support as indicated
Increase the long-term oxygen prescription on the basis of the initial saturation
why: A reading of 82 percent needs immediate assessment and verification rather than a routine delay.
Comfortable appearance does not establish adequate oxygenation; verify the measurement and clinical response.
Cold-site poor perfusion can distort a reading, but severe true hypoxaemia must be addressed promptly even when distress is not obvious.
An isolated potentially unreliable value does not authorize an unsupported long-term prescription change.
takeaway: Check the person and the measurement together.

title: Hypoglycemia while alert
stem: An adult with diabetes is alert, can swallow safely and has mild symptoms with glucose 3.5 mmol/L. Under the treatment protocol, what is appropriate?
options: Give a high-fat snack and recheck in an hour
Give 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate and recheck glucose in 15 minutes
Give 15 g of fast carbohydrate and wait until the next meal to check again
Give a large mixed meal first and reassess only if symptoms persist
why: Fat can slow carbohydrate absorption and an hour delays reassessment; use fast carbohydrate and timely recheck.
For mild to moderate hypoglycemia, fast-acting carbohydrate and reassessment are appropriate; repeat according to protocol if still low.
Treatment needs reassessment at 15 minutes and repetition as indicated.
A measured fast-acting carbohydrate treatment provides a more reliable initial response and requires rechecking.
takeaway: Treat, recheck and address the cause; oral treatment requires safe swallowing.

title: A seizure
stem: A client begins a generalized tonic-clonic seizure in bed. What should the nurse do?
options: Insert an oral airway during the convulsions to prevent tongue obstruction
Hold the shoulders and legs firmly to keep the client on the mattress
Protect from injury, time the seizure and support airway/safety according to protocol
Leave the bedside to obtain the full medication list before calling for help
why: Do not force equipment into the mouth during convulsions; protect the airway using safe protocol measures.
Forceful restraint can injure the client; use safe environmental protection.
Protect the head/environment, seek help and manage airway safely; escalate prolonged or repeated seizures.
Stay, protect and time the seizure while obtaining assistance; history should not delay safety measures.
takeaway: Protect, observe and support safety; do not restrain or put objects in the mouth.

title: Possible sepsis
stem: An adult with a suspected infection becomes confused, breathes rapidly and has a blood pressure of 84/48 mmHg. What is the priority?
options: Wait for culture results before activating the emergency pathway
Activate urgent assessment and treatment for possible sepsis/shock
Treat the fever first and repeat blood pressure after the antipyretic takes effect
Obtain the complete medication history before reporting possible sepsis
why: Diagnostic confirmation must not delay emergency assessment/treatment of possible sepsis and shock.
Infection with organ dysfunction and hypotension needs urgent care.
Hypotension and altered mental status indicate urgent instability rather than isolated fever.
History is useful but should not delay emergency escalation.
takeaway: Treat deterioration with suspected infection as time-critical.

title: Acute chest pain
stem: A client develops new crushing chest discomfort with sweating and shortness of breath. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Try the prescribed antacid and activate the pathway only if pain remains
Promptly assess and activate the chest-pain/emergency pathway
Wait for the first troponin result before notifying the emergency team
Review cardiac risk factors before deciding whether the symptom pattern is urgent
why: Possible acute coronary symptoms require prompt assessment and pathway activation rather than an antacid trial first.
This symptom pattern requires urgent assessment and protocol-based care.
Time-sensitive assessment and response should not wait for a laboratory result.
Age or a low known risk profile does not safely exclude an acute emergency.
takeaway: Respond to the pattern and urgency rather than making a reassuring assumption.

title: An unresponsive client
stem: A nurse finds an adult unresponsive and only gasping. No definite pulse is felt within 10 seconds. There is no applicable order limiting resuscitation. What is the appropriate immediate response?
options: Give rescue breaths only and wait for the emergency team before starting compressions
Activate emergency response, start high-quality CPR and use an AED as soon as it is available
Obtain a blood-pressure reading to confirm cardiac arrest before starting CPR
Wait until an AED arrives before starting chest compressions
why: With no definite pulse, CPR is indicated rather than ventilation alone.
No definite pulse within ten seconds with abnormal breathing is treated as cardiac arrest under healthcare-provider BLS guidance.
Further tests should not delay CPR when arrest has been identified.
Begin high-quality CPR while the AED is obtained.
takeaway: With abnormal breathing and no definite pulse within 10 seconds, activate emergency response, start CPR and use the AED promptly.

title: Acute shortness of breath
stem: A client becomes severely breathless while lying flat and coughs pink frothy sputum. What is the priority?
options: Increase the maintenance IV fluid because the client looks acutely unwell
Position to support breathing as tolerated, activate urgent help and assess/support oxygenation under protocol
Keep the client flat until a chest radiograph confirms the cause
Give the next routine oral diuretic and wait for its effect before calling for help
why: Unassessed fluid administration may worsen pulmonary congestion.
This may signal acute pulmonary edema and requires urgent respiratory/circulatory care.
Supine positioning can worsen breathing and diagnosis should not delay urgent support.
Severe respiratory distress needs immediate assessment/support, not delayed routine oral treatment.
takeaway: Severe respiratory distress takes priority over routine care.

title: Suspected pulmonary embolism
stem: A postoperative client suddenly develops dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain and tachycardia. What is the best response?
options: Treat the pain with the next oral analgesic and reassess before reporting
Activate urgent assessment, limit exertion and support breathing as indicated
Use coached breathing alone because postoperative anxiety is common
Arrange routine imaging and continue normal activity while waiting
why: Symptom treatment must not delay assessment of a possible acute cardiopulmonary emergency.
This pattern may indicate pulmonary embolism and needs prompt assessment.
Anxiety cannot be assumed to explain sudden dyspnea with pleuritic pain and tachycardia.
The client needs urgent assessment and limited exertion while supported.
takeaway: Sudden postoperative cardiopulmonary symptoms require urgent escalation.

title: Postpartum bleeding
stem: Soon after birth, a client has rapidly increasing vaginal bleeding, pallor and dizziness. What is the priority?
options: Weigh all used pads before calling for assistance
Activate the obstetric emergency response and immediately assess/support circulation under protocol
Help the client void first and reassess the bleeding afterward
Review the antenatal hemoglobin and coagulation results before activating the hemorrhage response
why: Quantification is useful but must not delay response to rapidly increasing bleeding with circulatory symptoms.
Possible postpartum hemorrhage is a time-critical emergency.
