Bladder management may form part of care, but possible hemorrhage requires emergency activation now.
Baseline results can inform treatment but must not delay emergency response to current rapid bleeding and circulatory symptoms.
takeaway: Judge bleeding by rate and the client’s condition, not by its presence alone.

title: Sudden airway obstruction
stem: A responsive, nonpregnant adult cannot speak, breathe or cough effectively after taking a bite of food. The nurse can encircle the adult’s abdomen. Under current adult basic life-support guidance, what should the nurse do?
options: Continue encouraging a cough without intervening because the client remains conscious
Start chest compressions while the client is still responsive and standing
Call for help and give repeated cycles of five back blows followed by five abdominal thrusts; switch to CPR if the client becomes unresponsive
Sweep the mouth with a finger before giving back blows, even when no object is visible
why: An ineffective cough with inability to speak or breathe indicates severe obstruction and needs trained action.
For a responsive adult with severe obstruction, begin the recommended choking manoeuvres; if unresponsive, follow the CPR pathway.
Current 2025 AHA adult guidance uses five back blows followed by five abdominal thrusts for responsive severe obstruction; special circumstances require modified technique.
Remove only a visible object; a blind sweep may worsen obstruction.
takeaway: Severe airway obstruction needs immediate trained action; use the unresponsive CPR pathway if consciousness is lost.

title: Recognizing dehydration
stem: Which findings can indicate significant volume depletion in an adult? Select all that apply.
options: Reduced urine output
Tachycardia with postural symptoms
One mildly dry mouth assessment without a change in intake, output or circulation
Hypotension with worsening weakness
A single normal blood-pressure value without symptoms or trend information
why: Reduced output may reflect impaired perfusion and needs assessment.
These may be compensatory and orthostatic signs.
An isolated dry mouth is nonspecific and does not by itself establish significant volume depletion.
This combination may indicate impaired circulation.
An isolated normal pressure is not evidence of significant volume depletion; assess the whole pattern.
takeaway: Combine losses, intake, vital signs and urine trends.

title: Severe hypoglycemia
stem: A client with diabetes is unresponsive and has a glucose of 2.1 mmol/L. Which action is appropriate?
options: Rub glucose gel inside the mouth because it does not need to be swallowed
Protect the airway, activate urgent help and give authorized non-oral glucose treatment under protocol
Prepare oral carbohydrate and give it as soon as the client briefly opens their eyes
Repeat the glucose after routine observations before starting treatment
why: An unconscious client cannot reliably protect the airway; use the authorized nonoral emergency pathway.
Severe hypoglycemia requires urgent treatment using an appropriate non-oral route, such as IV glucose or glucagon as authorized.
Brief eye opening does not establish safe swallowing; urgent nonoral treatment is appropriate.
A low result with unconsciousness requires immediate treatment and airway support, not a routine delay.
takeaway: Consciousness and swallowing safety determine whether oral treatment is suitable.

title: Recognizing respiratory distress
stem: Which observations warrant prompt assessment for respiratory deterioration? Select all that apply.
options: New inability to finish a sentence because of breathlessness
Marked use of accessory muscles
A respiratory rate of 18/min with normal effort and the client’s usual oxygen target met
New confusion with respiratory symptoms
Brief breathlessness after usual exertion that resolves promptly to the established baseline
why: Breathlessness that limits speech suggests significant distress.
Accessory muscle use can reflect increased work of breathing.
These findings are reassuring in this comparison; continue assessment in context.
Altered mental status can occur with severe hypoxia or hypercapnia.
This does not by itself demonstrate new acute deterioration, unlike the other listed red flags.
takeaway: Work of breathing and mental status matter as well as oxygen saturation.

title: Which report changes the priority?
stem: Four clients are receiving morning care. Which report requires the practical nurse to interrupt routine medication preparation and assess immediately?
options: A client with stable COPD is at their prescribed oxygen target and reports usual exertional breathlessness
A client taking an anticoagulant reports a new severe headache and vomiting after a fall last night
A client awaiting discharge has questions about a medication stopped yesterday
A client with arthritis requests their prescribed analgesic before physiotherapy
why: A stable finding at the client’s baseline needs ongoing care but is not the most urgent change.
Anticoagulation, recent head trauma and new neurological symptoms raise concern for intracranial bleeding.
Reconciliation and education are needed, but acute deterioration takes priority.
Pre-activity analgesia supports mobility but can wait briefly while the acute risk is assessed.
takeaway: Compare change from baseline and potential harm, not diagnosis labels alone.

title: Assignment after a change
stem: A care provider has safely assisted a client with walking for several days. Today the client reports new weakness and nearly falls when standing. What should the nurse do before the next walk?
options: Continue the same assignment because the worker is experienced
Ask the worker to document the change after the next walk
Reassess the client and revise the assistance and supervision plan
Ask a second unregulated worker to join without further assessment
why: Worker competence does not remove the need to reassess a changed client.
Documentation alone does not establish whether another walk is safe.
New weakness changes predictability and may change the required equipment or level of support.
More people do not substitute for an assessment of the new problem.
takeaway: An appropriate assignment can become inappropriate when the client changes.

title: An unresolved safety concern
stem: A nurse reports a sudden deterioration to the responsible clinician but receives instructions for routine observation only. The client continues to worsen. What is the best next action?
options: Repeat the original observations at the requested interval before making further contact
Continue immediate assessment/support and escalate through the urgent-response chain
Send a routine electronic message and wait for it to be acknowledged
Contact the unit manager after completing the scheduled medication round
why: Continuing deterioration invalidates waiting for routine reassessment.
Clear escalation with current findings is needed when the initial response does not address the evolving risk.
An asynchronous routine message may not provide the response needed for active deterioration.
Urgent assessment/support and escalation take priority over routine medication timing.
takeaway: Escalation continues until an unresolved safety concern receives an appropriate response.

title: A treatment disagreement
stem: A capable adult accepts symptom treatment but refuses a proposed blood transfusion. A family member insists it should proceed. What should guide the nurse’s response?
options: Request a family signature before acknowledging the client’s refusal
The client’s informed decision should be respected while alternatives and concerns are addressed
Treat acceptance of symptom care as implied consent to transfusion
Delay all symptom care until the client agrees to the transfusion
why: A capable adult’s informed refusal does not require family authorization.
Support understanding, communicate the refusal and collaborate on acceptable alternatives.
Consent is treatment-specific; agreement to one intervention does not authorize a refused transfusion.
Refusal of one treatment does not justify withholding acceptable indicated care.
takeaway: Capacity and informed choice matter more than agreement with the recommendation.

title: A factual progress note
stem: Which progress note most clearly communicates both analgesic response and current safety after an IV analgesic?
options: Thirty minutes after IV analgesic, client resting with eyes closed; pulse 84/min and BP 124/72 mm Hg; no further medicine requested
Thirty minutes after IV analgesic, client reports pain 3/10; temperature 36.8°C and dressing dry; plans to walk after lunch
Thirty minutes after IV analgesic, client reports pain decreased from 8/10 to 3/10; alert, respirations 16/min
Before IV analgesic, pain 8/10, alert and respirations 16/min; thirty minutes later, reports pain 3/10 and is sleeping
why: Resting and absence of a request do not directly quantify pain relief or establish current arousability and respiratory status.
The current pain report is useful, but wound and temperature findings do not provide the relevant sedation/respiratory reassessment.
This links the intervention interval to reported change and current alertness and respirations.
The earlier safety findings do not establish current respiratory status or whether the sleeping client is readily arousable.
takeaway: Document specific assessments and responses rather than vague judgments.

title: What does a signature mean?
stem: A client signs a procedure form, then asks whether they can change their mind before it begins. What is the best response?
options: You may withdraw only until the sterile equipment has been opened
We can record your concern, but the booked procedure must go ahead today
You can withdraw consent; let us discuss your concerns and notify the team
You must sign a second form before the team is allowed to pause
why: Preparation costs or equipment do not make consent irrevocable.
Scheduling does not override ongoing voluntary consent.
Acknowledge the right to reconsider and support an informed discussion.
An expressed withdrawal or concern should be acted on promptly; paperwork must not prevent a pause.
takeaway: Consent remains active before and during care.

title: Clarifying a telephone order
stem: Under a policy allowing telephone medication orders, the nurse cannot clearly hear the dose. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Ask the prescriber to repeat only the dose and document without read-back
Ask the prescriber to repeat and clarify, then read back the complete order according to policy
Enter the most likely dose as provisional so the medication can be prepared
Ask another nurse to listen to the nurse’s recollection of the call
why: Clarifying and reading back the complete order helps verify all elements and units.
Clarification and read-back help establish a complete, accurate order before implementation.
Unresolved medication ambiguity should not be converted into an actionable preparation.
A second person hearing an uncertain recollection does not verify the intended order at its source.
takeaway: Resolve communication ambiguity at the source.

title: A request to disclose information
stem: An adult client’s friend asks the nurse for investigation results. The client is alert and available, and no consent to disclose has been established. What should the nurse do?
options: Share normal results because they are less sensitive than abnormal findings
Confirm the client’s wishes and authorization before disclosing information
Assume permission because the friend drove the client to the appointment
Confirm that the friend is listed as an emergency contact and then share all results
why: Normal results are still protected health information.
Establish the client’s consent and the appropriate scope of disclosure.
Helping with transport does not establish consent to disclose test results.
Emergency-contact status does not automatically authorize unrestricted disclosure.
takeaway: Confirm permission, identity and purpose before disclosure.

title: Recognizing a dosing mismatch
stem: For a calculation exercise, an adult has a verified order for lorazepam 0.25 mg orally once. The supplied 0.5 mg tablet is approved for equal splitting, and clinical administration checks are complete. How many tablets equal the prescribed dose?
options: 2 tablets
0.5 tablet
1 tablet
0.25 tablet
why: This reverses the dose-to-strength relationship; two tablets would contain 1 mg.
0.25 mg divided by 0.5 mg/tablet equals half a tablet.
One tablet contains 0.5 mg, twice the prescribed 0.25 mg.
This treats the prescribed milligrams as the tablet fraction; a quarter tablet contains 0.125 mg.
takeaway: Divide the prescribed dose by the tablet strength, keeping the units visible; clinical appropriateness is a separate check.

title: A per-day order
stem: A child older than 2 years with uncomplicated acute otitis media weighs 20 kg. The verified prescription is amoxicillin 45 mg/kg/DAY orally, divided into three equal doses every 8 hours for 5 days. There is no penicillin allergy or renal impairment, and medication safety checks are complete. How many milligrams are prescribed for ONE dose?
options: 300 mg
900 mg
15 mg
why: 45 mg/kg/day × 20 kg = 900 mg/day; 900 ÷ 3 = 300 mg per dose.
900 mg is the total daily amount; divide it among three doses.
Dividing 45 mg/kg/day by three gives 15 mg/kg/dose; the child’s 20 kg weight must still be applied.
Multiplying the 900 mg daily total by three reverses the required division.
takeaway: Distinguish the total daily dose from each administration: 45 × 20 ÷ 3 = 300 mg per dose.

title: Before a scheduled dose
stem: A scheduled beta-blocker has a prescribed hold parameter for pulse below 55/min. The nurse obtains a pulse of 48/min and the client reports dizziness. What is best?
options: Give the medication because only the pulse, not the blood pressure, is below its parameter
Withhold according to the parameter, assess the client and contact the responsible clinician
Give half the dose so some beta-blocker effect is maintained
Recheck the pulse in an hour without assessing the dizziness or notifying the clinician
why: Each ordered hold parameter matters; adequate blood pressure does not cancel bradycardia.
Follow the prescribed limit and assess/escalate symptomatic bradycardia.
An unsupported dose reduction does not follow the hold order or address the symptoms.
The current symptomatic pulse below the parameter needs assessment and escalation.
takeaway: Use the actual prescribed parameters and assess the client, not just the number.

title: An IV site that burns
stem: A client receiving an IV vesicant reports burning, and swelling is visible near the cannula. What is the best immediate response?
options: Flush with a small saline volume to confirm whether the cannula remains patent
Stop the infusion, do not flush, retain the cannula initially and follow the medication-specific extravasation protocol
Remove the cannula immediately, then decide whether aspiration or an antidote is needed
Pause the infusion, apply a warm compress and restart at a lower rate if pain improves
why: Flushing may force more vesicant into tissue.
The line may be needed for aspiration or a specific treatment before removal; protocol details depend on the agent.
Removing access first can prevent useful aspiration or treatment through it.
Do not restart through suspected extravasation; compresses and treatment depend on the drug.
takeaway: Suspected extravasation is medication-specific: stop, do not flush, and follow the relevant protocol.

title: PPE based on the task
stem: A nurse will irrigate a wound where splashing of fluid is anticipated. Which protective approach is most appropriate?
options: Gloves and a gown, without face protection because splashes are expected to be small
Gloves, protective clothing and face/eye protection appropriate to the anticipated splash
Gloves and a surgical mask without eye protection
Gloves and ordinary prescription glasses without side protection
why: Anticipated splashes can reach eyes, nose and mouth even in small amounts.
Select barriers for the expected exposure of hands, clothing and face.
A mask alone does not protect the eyes from a splash.
Ordinary glasses are not equivalent to suitable protective eyewear for anticipated splashes.
takeaway: Anticipated exposure, not just a diagnosis, determines protective equipment.

title: A fall despite precautions
stem: A client who understands the call-bell instructions gets up alone at night to urgently urinate. Which revision best addresses the identified problem?
options: Repeat call-bell practice and add a reminder sign beside the bed
Assess toileting patterns and arrange timely assistance with accessible equipment
Add a bed-exit alarm and keep the existing assistance schedule
Offer a larger absorbent product and continue toileting at the established round times
why: The client already understands the call bell; more reminders do not address urgency or the timing of assistance.
The revised plan targets the activity and access problem that led to getting up alone.
An alarm may alert staff after movement begins but does not resolve predictable urgency or equipment access.
Containment may be useful, but it does not replace timely toileting assistance for the identified urgent need.
takeaway: A useful prevention plan addresses why the unsafe activity occurred.

title: A realistic teaching goal
stem: An adult’s asthma action plan prescribes inhaled fluticasone twice daily and inhaled salbutamol as needed for symptoms. The client now feels well. Which teach-back statement shows understanding of the different roles of these medicines?
options: I will take salbutamol twice daily for prevention and use fluticasone when sudden wheezing starts
I will continue fluticasone every day even when well and use salbutamol for symptoms as directed in my plan
I will stop fluticasone after a symptom-free week and restart it when wheezing returns
I will take extra fluticasone in place of salbutamol whenever I need quick symptom relief
why: This reverses the supplied controller and reliever roles.
Daily fluticasone controls airway inflammation; salbutamol is the prescribed symptom reliever in this plan.
The daily controller should not be stopped independently because symptoms improve.
Fluticasone alone is not the prescribed rapid reliever; follow the individualized plan and escalation instructions.
takeaway: Understand the role of each named inhaler in the individual action plan; do not stop a prescribed daily controller simply because symptoms improve.

title: Interpreting home measurements
stem: A client brings home blood-pressure readings taken immediately after climbing stairs with an incorrectly sized cuff. What is the best initial teaching focus?
options: Average all the readings without correcting technique first
Review correct technique, equipment fit and the prescribed monitoring/reporting plan
Repeat the readings with the same cuff immediately after sitting down
Record only readings that fall within the target range
why: Averaging systematically flawed measurements does not remove technique-related bias.
Improve measurement quality before interpreting the trend in collaboration with the care team.
Cuff fit and an appropriate rest period need correction, not merely a quick repeat.
Selective recording prevents an accurate pattern from being assessed.
takeaway: Reliable measurement comes before reliable trend interpretation.

title: A statement of hopelessness
stem: A client says they have collected pills and intend to take them tonight. What is the priority?
options: Give crisis contact information and arrange a later telephone check
Stay with the client, activate immediate safety support and restrict access to means when safe
Obtain a promise not to take the pills and use that promise to end observation
Leave the client alone briefly while finding a private room for a full interview
why: A stated imminent plan with means requires immediate safety support.
Intent, means and a near-term plan indicate serious immediate risk requiring protective support.
A promise is not a substitute for assessment and protective action.
Do not leave an imminently at-risk client alone; summon assistance while maintaining safety.
takeaway: Specific intent, means and timing change the urgency of the response.

title: Confusion or a long-term change?
stem: An older adult with mild, stable dementia becomes acutely inattentive and fluctuates between drowsiness and agitation after surgery. What is most appropriate?
options: Continue the dementia care plan because postoperative disorientation is expected
Assess for delirium and reversible contributors, and communicate the acute change
Request sedation as the first response without checking pain, oxygenation or other reversible contributors
Wait for the family to confirm a baseline change before reporting the new findings
why: Acute fluctuating inattention requires assessment for delirium and causes.
Acute inattention and fluctuating consciousness suggest delirium requiring assessment of causes.
Symptom suppression alone can miss the underlying acute illness.
Collateral history helps, but observed acute change warrants prompt assessment and communication.
takeaway: A chronic diagnosis does not explain every new finding.

title: Reassessing pain before mobilization
stem: A client reports incisional pain of 7/10 and refuses planned postoperative walking. Which response best balances comfort and recovery?
options: Substitute bed exercises for today’s walking session and retain the same pain plan
Assess the barriers, provide prescribed relief and reassess graded walking with the client
Shorten the walking distance and attempt it before the prescribed analgesic takes effect
Give the prescribed analgesic and record the mobility goal as achieved if pain improves
why: Bed exercises may be appropriate temporarily, but automatically substituting them leaves the modifiable pain barrier and walking goal unresolved.
This addresses the limiting symptom, respects participation and evaluates what activity becomes safely achievable.
A shorter distance may help, but attempting it before agreed relief is effective does not address the reason for refusal.
Improved pain is not proof that safe walking or the functional goal has been achieved.
takeaway: Use comfort interventions to enable function, then evaluate both.

title: A change in skin integrity
stem: A client with reduced mobility has intact skin over the sacrum that remains red and does not blanch with gentle pressure. What is the best response?
options: Massage the area before applying a barrier product
Relieve pressure and reassess/document the skin while updating the prevention plan
Apply a protective dressing and keep the current repositioning plan unchanged
Use a ring-shaped cushion to keep the red area in the centre
why: Massage may damage compromised tissue; relieve pressure and manage contributing factors.
Persistent non-blanchable redness is an important early warning requiring pressure relief and follow-up.
A dressing alone does not address ongoing pressure or the need to reassess the plan.
Ring-shaped devices can create pressure at the edges and are not an appropriate substitute for assessed offloading.
takeaway: Act on intact-skin pressure damage with offloading and assessment; colour changes may be less obvious in dark skin, so assess temperature, firmness, pain and the full skin context.

title: Distinguishing baseline from deterioration
stem: A client with heart failure has the following observations. Which change is the highest priority to report after immediate assessment?
options: A usual mild ankle swelling that resolves overnight
New breathlessness at rest with oxygen saturation below the prescribed target
A request to review the low-sodium meal choices
An unchanged daily weight taken on the same scale
why: A stable baseline finding needs monitoring but is less urgent than new respiratory compromise.
New resting dyspnea and a low saturation suggest acute respiratory deterioration.
Nutrition teaching can follow assessment of the urgent symptom.
A stable weight does not rule out a new acute problem.
takeaway: A stable trend in one measure does not cancel a new red-flag symptom.

title: A laboratory result in context
stem: A client receiving anticoagulation has new black tarry stools and dizziness. Which action is most appropriate?
options: Wait for the scheduled INR because bleeding severity can be judged from that result
Assess circulation and symptoms and promptly escalate possible bleeding
Ask about iron supplements and stop the assessment if the client takes one
Arrange a routine stool test and defer escalation until it is positive
why: Symptoms require assessment now; INR is not relevant to every anticoagulant and does not rule out bleeding.
Melena and dizziness may indicate clinically significant gastrointestinal bleeding.
Iron can darken stools, but tarry stools with dizziness while anticoagulated require assessment for bleeding.
Clinical concern should prompt timely assessment and escalation without waiting for routine testing.
takeaway: Symptoms can require urgent action before a scheduled laboratory check.

title: What changes the immediate plan?
stem: A client with low glucose is initially awake but becomes too drowsy to swallow safely while oral treatment is being prepared. What should the nurse do?
options: Use glucose gel in the cheek because the client no longer needs to drink
Change to the authorized non-oral emergency pathway and support the airway
Give small spoonfuls while holding the client upright
Repeat the glucose before activating a different treatment pathway
why: Reduced consciousness makes airway protection unreliable; use the authorized nonoral pathway.
A loss of safe swallowing changes the route and urgency of treatment.
Position and slower delivery do not establish safe swallowing in deteriorating alertness.
Deterioration while known hypoglycemia is being treated requires immediate safety and treatment changes.
takeaway: Reassess while preparing treatment; a change in condition may invalidate the original plan.

title: Conflicting priorities
stem: A postoperative client reports sudden dyspnea and looks pale. The nurse is about to give the client’s routine oral medicines. What is the best initial action?
options: Give the oral medicines while asking another staff member to check oxygen saturation
Stop the routine task, assess airway/breathing/circulation and summon appropriate help
Check the medication list for a likely adverse effect before attending to breathing
Coach slow breathing first and assess only if the symptoms do not resolve
why: New dyspnea requires immediate assessment and may make oral administration unsafe.
A new acute change requires prompt assessment and appropriate emergency escalation.
Cause investigation should not delay immediate airway/breathing/circulation assessment.
Reassurance or breathing coaching alone can miss an acute physiological emergency.
takeaway: Change priorities when the client changes.
